items.q: Alpaydin Exercise 7.1 uses k-means for **image compression** (vector quantization): the image is split into windows, k-means clusters them, and only the reference vectors + indices are sent. The k centroids act as:
options: a codebook; each window is encoded by the index of its nearest centroid
items.explain: K-means is vector quantization: the k centroids form a codebook, and each block is replaced by its nearest centroid's index — compressing the data. (Alpaydin Ex 7.1.)

items.q: Alpaydin treats k-means as a special case of the EM algorithm for a mixture model. K-means corresponds to EM with:
options: hard (0/1) assignments and equal spherical covariances
items.explain: K-means = EM with hard assignments and equal spherical covariances (and equal priors); the assignment step is the E-step, the mean update is the M-step. (Alpaydin §7.4.)

items.q: Alpaydin Exercise 7.4 asks you to define a **multivariate Bernoulli mixture** (binary inputs) and derive its EM equations. This shows EM/clustering extends to:
options: discrete/binary features via a Bernoulli mixture
items.explain: EM is general: with binary inputs you use a Bernoulli mixture (the discrete analogue of a Gaussian mixture) and derive analogous E/M updates. (Alpaydin Ex 7.4.)

items.q: Alpaydin Exercise 6.2: implementing PCA and reconstructing digit images, the reconstruction error as the number of retained eigenvectors increases:
items.explain: More principal components capture more variance, so reconstruction error falls as you keep more eigenvectors — a principled way to choose k. (Alpaydin Ex 6.2.)

items.q: In Alpaydin's treatment, the principal components are the eigenvectors of the covariance matrix, ordered so that the FIRST captures:
items.explain: PCA projects onto the eigenvectors with the largest eigenvalues; PC1 captures maximum variance, PC2 the next (orthogonal) direction, etc. (Alpaydin §6.3.)

items.q: Alpaydin contrasts feature **selection** (subset selection) with feature **extraction** (PCA). The key difference is that PCA:
options: creates new features that are combinations of the originals
items.explain: Subset selection keeps a subset of original features (losing the rest); PCA extracts new features that are linear combinations of all originals, retaining more signal. (Alpaydin Ch 6.)

items.q: Mitchell models reinforcement learning as a Markov Decision Process. The agent's goal is to learn a policy π that:
options: maximizes the cumulative discounted reward (return) from every state
items.explain: The objective is a policy maximizing expected cumulative discounted reward $\sum \gamma^t r_t$. (Mitchell Ch 13.)

items.q: Mitchell defines the Q function as $Q(s,a) = r(s,a) + \gamma V^*(\delta(s,a))$. The optimal policy is then:
items.explain: Q(s,a) is the value of taking action a then acting optimally; the optimal policy greedily picks $\arg\max_a Q(s,a)$, and $V^*(s)=\max_a Q(s,a)$. (Mitchell §13.3.)

items.q: Mitchell Exercise 13.2: in a deterministic grid world with γ=0.8 and Q initialized to 0, after the first episode the Q-learning update modifies:
options: mainly the Q value for the transition INTO the goal (then values propagate backward in later episodes)
items.explain: With Q=0 everywhere, only transitions whose successor has non-zero value (i.e. into the goal) get updated first; subsequent episodes propagate value backward one step at a time. (Mitchell Ex 13.2.)

items.q: Mitchell Exercise 13.3 formulates Tic-Tac-Toe vs a random opponent as a Q-learning task. Because the opponent is random, the environment is a:
items.explain: A random opponent makes state transitions stochastic → a non-deterministic MDP; states = board positions, rewards on win/lose/draw. (Mitchell Ex 13.3.)

items.q: Mitchell Exercise 13.4: even when one policy beats another from some states but loses from others, an MDP always has:
options: a single optimal policy π* that maximizes V^π(s) for EVERY state s
items.explain: A fundamental MDP result: there always exists an optimal policy π* that is simultaneously best from every starting state. (Mitchell Ex 13.4.)

items.q: Mitchell's Q-learning is called **model-free** because the agent:
options: knows the transition and reward functions
learns Q directly from experience without knowing δ(s,a) or r(s,a)
items.explain: Q-learning estimates Q from sampled transitions (s,a,r,s') without an explicit model of transitions/rewards — model-free, off-policy. (Mitchell §13.3.)

items.q: Alpaydin Exercise 7.2 warns against doing k-means, partitioning instances, then estimating the covariance Sᵢ separately per group. The problem is that:
options: the hard partition ignores assignment uncertainty, biasing the estimates (soft EM is preferable)
items.explain: Hard partitioning then estimating per-cluster covariance ignores the uncertainty in assignments, giving biased estimates; soft EM with responsibilities is more principled. (Alpaydin Ex 7.2.)

items.q: PCA can be computed via SVD of the centered data matrix X, where the principal components are the right singular vectors and the eigenvalues relate to singular values by:
items.explain: The covariance ∝ XᵀX, whose eigenvalues are the squares of X's singular values: $\lambda_i = \sigma_i^2$. So PCA ≡ SVD of the centered data. (Standard linear-algebra result; Alpaydin Ch 6.)
